results.title: [PDF] When is TSLS Actually LATE?
results.content: Christine Blandhol, John Bonney, Magne Mogstad, and Alexander Torgovitsky NBER Working Paper No. 29709 January 2022, Revised January 2025 JEL No. C26 ABSTRACT Linear instrumental variable estimators, such as two-stage least squares (TSLS), are commonly interpreted as estimating non-negatively weighted averages of causal effects, referred to as local average treatment effects (LATEs). Since the work of Imbens and Angrist (1994), it has been increasingly common to interpret linear IV estimators as estimating a local average treatment eﬀect (LATE), or at least a non-negatively weighted average of LATEs. The LATE interpretation is most commonly derived for simpliﬁed IV speciﬁcations that do not include covariates.

Title: Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) Calculator
Run this analysis with our Local Average Treatment Effect Calculator. The Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) estimates the causal effect of a treatment for the subpopulation of **compliers** — individuals who take the treatment when assigned to it and abstain when assigned to control. Identified through an instrumental variable (IV), LATE is the central estimand in randomized trials with imperfect compliance and in natural experiments with partial take-up. * LATE scales the intention-to-treat (ITT) effect by the compliance rate difference (Wald estimator). * It applies only to compliers — not to always-takers or never-takers. * A first-stage F-statistic below 10 signals a weak instrument and unreliable LATE estimates. * Sensitivity analysis quantifies how robust the estimate is to violations of the exclusion restriction. LATE resolves this by using random assignment as an instrument for uptake, recovering the causal effect among those whose behaviour the instrument actually changes — the compliers. The denominator \Delta\_c is the compliance rate in the treatment arm minus that in the control arm, equal to the proportion of compliers. Dividing scales the ITT up to the per-treatment effect for compliers. 3. Estimate the compliance difference: take-up rate in treatment arm minus take-up rate in control arm. For example, with a 65% treatment-arm take-up and 10% crossover in controls, the compliance difference is 0.55 and LATE is ~1.82 times the ITT. The Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) is the causal effect of a treatment for the subpopulation of compliers — individuals whose treatment status is changed by the instrument. It is identified by the Wald/IV estimator as the ratio of the intention-to-treat (ITT) effect on the outcome to the ITT effect on treatment compliance. LATE is the relevant estimand in randomized trials with non-compliance and in natural experiments where only a subset of the population responds to the instrumental variable. Under monotonicity, the population is divided into three principal strata: compliers (proportion = compliance difference, the people for whom LATE is estimated), always-takers (proportion = crossover rate in the control arm, people who take treatment regardless of assignment), and never-takers (proportion = 1 − compliance rate in the treatment arm, people who refuse treatment regardless of assignment).

results.content: We propose an instrumental-variable (IV) approach to estimate the causal effect of service satisfaction on customer loyalty, by exploiting a common source of randomness in the assignment of service employees to customers in service queues. results.title: Estimand
results.content: **An estimand is a key concept in statistical inference: the quantity of interest that a researcher aims to estimate.**. An estimand is a concept in statistics that *defines* to the quantity of interest that a researcher aims to estimate using statistical methods. The concept of an estimand is particularly important in causal inference, where the goal is to estimate the causal effect of an intervention or treatment on an outcome variable. In this context, the estimand specifies what the causal effect is, in terms of the population parameter that represents the effect. An Average Treatment Effect (ATE) estimand is a commonly used concept in causal inference that aims to estimate the **average** causal effect of a treatment or intervention on an outcome variable in a population. The ATE estimand is defined as the difference between the average outcome of the treated group and the average outcome of the control group, where the treatment status is randomly assigned to the study participants.

results.content: This is possible as long as examiners are randomly assigned and there is sufﬁcient variation in examiners’ propensities to assign the various treatments.28 As discussed in Section 5, the constant effects assumption can be relaxed in the case of a single binary treatment, if a monotonicity condition holds, and IV identiﬁes a local weighted av-erage treatment effect among compliers (Imbens and Angrist, 1994). A simple linear regression shows that defendants are 3 percentage points more likely to be released pretrial if they were assigned to a judge whose estimated release rate was 10 percentage points higher.34 As detailed in Section 5.2, IV estimates of the parameter δ can be interpreted as a weighted average of the causal effects of pre-trial release when there is treatment effect heterogeneity and the assumptions of instrument exogeneity, exclusion, and monotonicity hold. If random assignment and strict exclusion hold, two examiners with the same propensity to treat can only have different average individual outcomes if they differ in the set of individuals whom they assign to treatment (a violation of pairwise monotonicity).
